items.stem: In eAssessment Task 2, students usually choose from:
items.answer: three visual prompts
items.markingKey: C. Three images are offered.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a cracked smartphone screen lit up in the dark, showing 47 unread messages.]
Image 2: [A photograph: snow falling on a market in Kraków; a stallholder pours hot chocolate for a girl who is counting coins.]
Image 3: [A photograph: an abandoned greenhouse in Iceland, its glass broken, with tomatoes still growing wild inside.]

Choose ONE image. Describe the mood it creates and suggest two different story ideas it could inspire, explaining whose perspective you would tell each from.
items.answer: Image 1: mood – tense and anxious; ideas – a rumour spreading online, a message that cannot be taken back, or an emergency at home | Image 2: mood – cosy but poignant; ideas – a small kindness, a girl saving for a present, or a stallholder's memory of his own childhood | Image 3: mood – mysterious and hopeful; ideas – life continuing after people leave, a family returning to their old farm, or a secret garden
items.markingKey: Indicative content (any image): Image 1: mood – tense and anxious; ideas – a rumour spreading online, a message that cannot be taken back, or an emergency at home | Image 2: mood – cosy but poignant; ideas – a small kindness, a girl saving for a present, or a stallholder's memory of his own childhood | Image 3: mood – mysterious and hopeful; ideas – life continuing after people leave, a family returning to their old farm, or a secret garden Marks: mood identified and justified from details (2); two plausible ideas (2); perspective explained (1).

items.stem: Priya writes: "The mood of your piece must match the image." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Writing against the image's mood – a joyful memory in a bleak setting – can be powerful.
items.markingKey: Writing against the image's mood – a joyful memory in a bleak setting – can be powerful. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: two hands, one old and one young, holding the same chess piece above a board in a park in Moscow.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]
Image 3: [A photograph: a flooded street in a coastal town; a dog sits on the roof of a floating car, looking at the camera.]

Choose ONE image. Plan a piece of creative writing: give a title, the form (story, diary, letter or speech), the opening hook, the turning point, the ending and the register you will use.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques: symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques: symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: An image shows a suitcase left on an empty railway platform at dusk. Give one literal and three inferential readings.
items.answer: Literal: a suitcase alone on a platform at dusk. Inferential: someone left in a hurry; someone is waiting to return; a refugee's only possessions; a decision not to leave. Credit three distinct inferences.
items.markingKey: Literal: a suitcase alone on a platform at dusk. Inferential: someone left in a hurry; someone is waiting to return; a refugee's only possessions; a decision not to leave. Credit three distinct inferences.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The best Task 2 responses ignore the obvious interpretation of the image."
items.answer: Originality helps, but control and insight matter most; a familiar idea told with skill can outperform a strange but weak one.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: originality is rewarded; unexpected angles engage readers. Arguments against: an obvious idea, well executed, can be powerful; forced originality can feel artificial. Supported judgement: Originality helps, but control and insight matter most; a familiar idea told with skill can outperform a strange but weak one.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "perspective".
items.answer: Whose point of view a piece is told from – a person in the image, an object, an outsider
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: whose point of view a piece is told from – a person in the image, an object, an outsider. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "sensory detail".
items.answer: Description that appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: description that appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Good stories use a lot of dialogue." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dialogue should be purposeful and limited in short pieces; a few lines with subtext are more effective than long exchanges.
items.markingKey: Dialogue should be purposeful and limited in short pieces; a few lines with subtext are more effective than long exchanges. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why dialogue should contain subtext.
items.answer: People rarely say exactly what they feel; subtext makes dialogue realistic and lets readers sense deeper tensions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: People rarely say exactly what they feel; subtext makes dialogue realistic and lets readers sense deeper tensions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story in which two siblings argue.

"You can't sell it," Leo said. "It's Dad's."
"It was Dad's." Mira didn't look up from the laptop. "Now it's a car that needs new brakes."
Leo picked at the peeling sticker on the fridge – a football club Dad had supported, badly, for forty years.
"He sang in that car," Leo said.
Mira's typing stopped. For a long moment there was only the hum of the fridge.
"I know," she said. "I know he did."

Explain how subtext works in the dialogue of this extract.
items.answer: Dialogue reveals character and conflict: Leo speaks emotionally, Mira practically, and the subtext is their shared grief for their father. The repeated "I know" shows Mira finally letting her feelings through.
items.markingKey: Dialogue reveals character and conflict: Leo speaks emotionally, Mira practically, and the subtext is their shared grief for their father. The repeated "I know" shows Mira finally letting her feelings through. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a young-adult novel about exam results day.

Mei read the email three times. A, A, B. The B sat at the end of the line like a stone in a shoe.
Downstairs, her mother was already on the phone to Auntie Lin, laughing her company laugh. "Of course she did well," she was saying. "Mei always does well."
Mei closed the laptop. She thought about the art portfolio hidden under her bed – the one nobody had asked to see – and, for the first time, she wondered whose results these really were.

Explain how "she wondered whose results these really were" shows a character's feelings without stating them.
items.answer: Rhetorical final thought: "she wondered whose results these really were" – the question marks the start of Mei's growing independence, a key coming-of-age moment.
items.markingKey: Rhetorical final thought: "she wondered whose results these really were" – the question marks the start of Mei's growing independence, a key coming-of-age moment. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a crowded night market in Bangkok seen from above; one stall glows brighter than the rest, and a boy stands still in the moving crowd.]

Write a story of about 300 words inspired by this image.
items.answer: Indicative content: a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; structure – sensory overload – a moment of stillness and loss – reunion or decision; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; structure – sensory overload – a moment of stillness and loss – reunion or decision; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Dialogue is the most effective way to reveal character."
items.answer: Dialogue is powerful, but it works best combined with action and detail that show what characters cannot say.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: speech reveals voice and relationships; subtext adds depth. Arguments against: actions and thoughts can reveal more; too much dialogue slows short pieces. Supported judgement: Dialogue is powerful, but it works best combined with action and detail that show what characters cannot say.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a schoolbag left on a bench at a bus stop in heavy rain; the bus's red tail-lights disappear around the corner.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a crowd of students marching with hand-painted placards that read "THERE IS NO PLANET B"; one younger girl is on her father's shoulders.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a cracked smartphone screen lit up in the dark, showing 47 unread messages.]

Write a creative piece of 400-600 words inspired by ONE of the images. You may write a story, a diary entry, a letter or a speech.
items.answer: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; a first-person narrator; structure: the missed bus – opening the bag – an unexpected consequence; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image.
items.markingKey: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; a first-person narrator; structure: the missed bus – opening the bag – an unexpected consequence; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story in which two siblings argue.

"You can't sell it," Leo said. "It's Dad's."
"It was Dad's." Mira didn't look up from the laptop. "Now it's a car that needs new brakes."
Leo picked at the peeling sticker on the fridge – a football club Dad had supported, badly, for forty years.
"He sang in that car," Leo said.
Mira's typing stopped. For a long moment there was only the hum of the fridge.
"I know," she said. "I know he did."

Rewrite the scene from Mira's point of view in the first person (about 250 words), keeping the subtext: do not use the words "sad" or "grief".
items.answer: Indicative content: first-person Mira; practical surface thoughts; hints of suppressed grief through action and sensory detail; correctly punctuated dialogue; subtext rather than statement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: first-person Mira; practical surface thoughts; hints of suppressed grief through action and sensory detail; correctly punctuated dialogue; subtext rather than statement. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The level of formality of language, chosen for audience and purpose"?
items.answer: register
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of register.

items.stem: Briefly explain why choosing a form is part of creative insight in Task 2.
items.answer: The form shapes voice, structure and audience; an unexpected form (a letter from the swing) can transform an image.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The form shapes voice, structure and audience; an unexpected form (a letter from the swing) can transform an image. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Stories are always the best choice for Task 2." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Letters, diaries, speeches or monologues can show insight and control if their conventions are used purposefully.
items.markingKey: Letters, diaries, speeches or monologues can show insight and control if their conventions are used purposefully. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following letter written in 1962 by a young woman who had recently emigrated, to her sister.

Dear Nalini,
The flat is small and the radiator knocks all night like a neighbour who wants to come in. At the factory they call me "Nelly" because they cannot say my name. I let them.
I have found a shop that sells cardamom, but it tastes of the box it came in.
Do not tell Amma I cry on the bus. Tell her I have a warm coat and that the English are polite. Both are true.
Your loving sister,
Saroja

Identify the text type of this extract and explain how two of its conventions are used.
items.answer: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "it tastes of the box it came in" (sensory detail) and letter conventions (salutation, sign-off), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "it tastes of the box it came in" (sensory detail) and letter conventions (salutation, sign-off), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in a formal register for a letter to a newspaper: "Honestly, the new bus timetable is a total joke and nobody can get to school on time."
items.answer: E.g. "The new bus timetable has made it very difficult for students to arrive at school on time." Credit formal vocabulary and removal of slang.
items.markingKey: E.g. "The new bus timetable has made it very difficult for students to arrive at school on time." Credit formal vocabulary and removal of slang.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: an empty playground swing still moving in thick fog; a single red glove lies on the wet tarmac.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a robot vacuum cleaner stuck against a door in a dark flat; the door is open just a crack, letting in light.]
Image 3: [A drawing: a staircase that spirals up into the clouds; at the bottom, a pair of school shoes has been left neatly side by side.]

Choose ONE image. Plan a piece of creative writing: give a title, the form (story, diary, letter or speech), the opening hook, the turning point, the ending and the register you will use.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: short story; narrator: a first-person narrator; structure: calm opening in the fog – discovery of the glove – revelation of who left it; techniques: pathetic fallacy, a recurring colour motif (red against grey), short sentences for tension. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: short story; narrator: a first-person narrator; structure: calm opening in the fog – discovery of the glove – revelation of who left it; techniques: pathetic fallacy, a recurring colour motif (red against grey), short sentences for tension. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: Explain why register must be consistent within a piece.
items.answer: Sudden shifts in formality break the voice and confuse the reader unless done deliberately for effect.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sudden shifts in formality break the voice and confuse the reader unless done deliberately for effect. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which is correct?
options: Each of the students having a torch.
Each of the students have a torch.
Each of the students has a torch.
Each of the student have a torch.
items.answer: Each of the students has a torch.
items.markingKey: C. "Each" is singular.

items.stem: Explain why comma splices are a problem.
items.answer: They blur the boundary between complete thoughts, making writing harder to follow and showing weak control of sentence structure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They blur the boundary between complete thoughts, making writing harder to follow and showing weak control of sentence structure. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
A student wrote: Despite the rain. We decided to walk to the station.
The corrected version is: Despite the rain, we decided to walk to the station.
Explain the rule that has been applied.
items.answer: Sentence fragment joined to its main clause with a comma.
items.markingKey: sentence fragment joined to its main clause with a comma. 1 mark for naming the error, 1 for explaining the rule.

items.stem: Edit this sentence for style and accuracy: "The sky was really really dark and the rain was falling down very hard."
items.answer: E.g. "Rain hammered from a sky as dark as wet slate." Credit precise verb, imagery and removal of repetition.
items.markingKey: E.g. "Rain hammered from a sky as dark as wet slate." Credit precise verb, imagery and removal of repetition.

items.stem: Rewrite the following to make it more precise and effective: I walked into the room. I saw a table. I saw a chair. I sat down.
items.answer: E.g. I walked into the room, past an empty table, and sank into the only chair.
items.markingKey: Example: I walked into the room, past an empty table, and sank into the only chair. (choppy, repetitive sentences combined for flow, with a stronger verb ("sank")). Credit any edit that removes repetition or vagueness and uses precise vocabulary and varied structure (criterion D).

items.stem: Write a 300-word piece inspired by an image, then annotate three edits you would make to improve its accuracy and style, explaining each.
items.answer: Indicative content: a controlled creative piece; three specific edits (accuracy and style) with explanations linked to criterion D. Criteria C and D.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a controlled creative piece; three specific edits (accuracy and style) with explanations linked to criterion D. Criteria C and D.

items.stem: Identify and correct the error(s) in: The crowd were silent, they waited, nobody moved.
items.answer: The crowd was silent. They waited. Nobody moved.
items.markingKey: The crowd was silent. They waited. Nobody moved. Error: comma splices replaced with full stops; short sentences for tension. 1 mark for the correction; 1 mark for identifying the error.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pacing"?
options: An image used as a stimulus for creative writing, as in eAssessment Task 2
The speed of a narrative, controlled by sentence length, detail and scene choice
Revealing feelings and character through action, detail and dialogue rather than stating them
The MYP criterion for using language: vocabulary, sentence structures, register, accuracy
items.answer: The speed of a narrative, controlled by sentence length, detail and scene choice
items.markingKey: B. "pacing" is the speed of a narrative, controlled by sentence length, detail and scene choice.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mood"?
options: The feeling an image or piece of writing creates
Description that appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch
The verb must match its subject in number ("each has", "they have")
Checking a finished text for errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar
items.answer: The feeling an image or piece of writing creates
items.markingKey: A. "mood" is the feeling an image or piece of writing creates.

items.stem: Explain the difference between formal register and informal register.
items.answer: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and no slang; informal register is conversational, with contractions and colloquial words.
items.markingKey: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and no slang; informal register is conversational, with contractions and colloquial words. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between an accidental fragment and a deliberate fragment.
items.answer: A deliberate fragment is used for effect ("She jumped."); an accidental fragment is an incomplete sentence that should be joined to a main clause.
items.markingKey: A deliberate fragment is used for effect ("She jumped."); an accidental fragment is an incomplete sentence that should be joined to a main clause. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between dialogue and reported speech.
items.answer: Dialogue gives characters' exact words in speech marks; reported speech summarises what was said ("He said that he was tired").
items.markingKey: Dialogue gives characters' exact words in speech marks; reported speech summarises what was said ("He said that he was tired"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a literal reading and an inferential reading.
items.answer: A literal reading describes what is shown; an inferential reading interprets what it suggests about story, character and feeling.
items.markingKey: A literal reading describes what is shown; an inferential reading interprets what it suggests about story, character and feeling. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between formal register and informal register.
items.answer: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and no slang; informal register is conversational, with contractions and colloquial words.
items.markingKey: Formal register uses complete sentences, precise vocabulary and no slang; informal register is conversational, with contractions and colloquial words. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Spell-check catches all errors." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Spell-check misses homophones (their/there), missing words and grammar errors; careful proofreading is needed.
items.markingKey: Spell-check misses homophones (their/there), missing words and grammar errors; careful proofreading is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Rewrite "Sam was terrified of the exam" to show rather than tell.
items.answer: E.g. "Sam read the first question three times. The words slid away. Under the desk, his knee would not stop bouncing." Credit action/detail implying fear.
items.markingKey: E.g. "Sam read the first question three times. The words slid away. Under the desk, his knee would not stop bouncing." Credit action/detail implying fear.

items.stem: "The mood of your piece must match the image." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Writing against the image's mood – a joyful memory in a bleak setting – can be powerful.
items.markingKey: Writing against the image's mood – a joyful memory in a bleak setting – can be powerful. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following letter from a student to her local council in Manchester.

Dear Councillor Patel,
I am writing to ask you to reconsider the decision to close Levenshulme Library.
For many students in my area, the library is the only quiet place to study. My flat has five people and one table. The library has Wi-Fi, printers and Mrs Okafor, who has helped me with every homework project since I was eight.
Closing it would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future.
I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group to discuss alternatives.
Yours sincerely,
Amira Hassan (age 14)

Identify the text type of this extract and explain how two of its conventions are used.
items.answer: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future" (antithesis) and stating the purpose in the first sentence, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a letter. Conventions: an address or salutation, a clear purpose in the opening, paragraphs that develop the case and a sign-off. In this text, for example: "would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future" (antithesis) and stating the purpose in the first sentence, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Proofread and correct the following sentence: Me and Leo should of stayed at home.
items.answer: Leo and I should have stayed at home.
items.markingKey: Leo and I should have stayed at home. Error: "Me and Leo" as subject → "Leo and I"; "should of" → "should have". 1 mark for the correction; 1 mark for identifying the error.

items.stem: Write a narrative of 400–600 words in which a character receives unexpected news. Show the character's feelings through action, detail and dialogue, and control the pace at the key moment.
items.answer: Indicative content: showing not telling; purposeful dialogue with subtext; varied pacing (slowing at the climax); sensory detail; correctly punctuated speech; deliberate structure. Criteria B, C, D.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: showing not telling; purposeful dialogue with subtext; varied pacing (slowing at the climax); sensory detail; correctly punctuated speech; deliberate structure. Criteria B, C, D.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a crowded night market in Bangkok seen from above; one stall glows brighter than the rest, and a boy stands still in the moving crowd.]

Write the opening paragraph (about 150 words) of a story inspired by this image. Hook the reader and establish the mood.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood; possible idea – a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a busy, vibrant but slightly lonely mood; possible idea – a boy separated from his family, a stallholder's last night before the market closes, or a newcomer to the city; techniques such as sensory lists, contrast between motion and stillness, a shift in pace; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: "Unusual forms score higher in creative writing than stories." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Form should be chosen for purpose; an unusual form helps only if its conventions are used with control.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they show originality; they stand out to examiners. Arguments against: a well-crafted story can show equal insight; unusual forms done poorly lose marks. Supported judgement: Form should be chosen for purpose; an unusual form helps only if its conventions are used with control. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which is correctly punctuated dialogue?
items.answer: "You can't sell it," Leo said.
items.markingKey: B. Comma inside speech marks before the tag.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "What an image suggests about story, character, mood or theme"?
items.answer: inferential reading
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of inferential reading.

items.stem: "Stories are always the best choice for Task 2." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Letters, diaries, speeches or monologues can show insight and control if their conventions are used purposefully.
items.markingKey: Letters, diaries, speeches or monologues can show insight and control if their conventions are used purposefully. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why you should leave time to proofread in the eAssessment.
items.answer: Errors in punctuation and grammar can lower criterion D marks; a few minutes of checking can correct many of them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Errors in punctuation and grammar can lower criterion D marks; a few minutes of checking can correct many of them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between telling and showing.
items.answer: Showing reveals through detail, action and dialogue ("her hands shook"); telling states directly ("she was nervous").
items.markingKey: Showing reveals through detail, action and dialogue ("her hands shook"); telling states directly ("she was nervous"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why brainstorming several ideas from an image is useful.
items.answer: The first idea is often obvious; generating several allows the writer to choose the most original and developed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The first idea is often obvious; generating several allows the writer to choose the most original and developed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a diary entry. Conventions: a date, a first-person private voice, the present moment and honest feelings. In this text, for example: "a rainbow sitting on it like a crown" (simile) and the turning point "Then the clouds split open", each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.

In this text, for example: "a rainbow sitting on it like a crown" (simile) and the turning point "Then the clouds split open", each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Rewrite the following to make it more precise and effective: She said she was sad. She said she wanted to go home. She said she missed her mum.
items.answer: E.g. "I want to go home," she whispered. "I miss Mum."
items.markingKey: Example: "I want to go home," she whispered. "I miss Mum." (repetitive reported speech replaced by dialogue that shows emotion). Credit any edit that removes repetition or vagueness and uses precise vocabulary and varied structure (criterion D).

items.stem: Priya writes: "Showing means adding as many adjectives as possible." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Showing relies on precise actions and telling details, not piles of adjectives.
items.markingKey: Showing relies on precise actions and telling details, not piles of adjectives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Suggest three different perspectives from which you could write about an image of a lighthouse in a storm, with the story each would tell.
items.answer: E.g. the keeper (duty and isolation); a sailor in the storm (fear, hope); the lighthouse itself (centuries of watching). Credit three perspectives with stories.
items.markingKey: E.g. the keeper (duty and isolation); a sailor in the storm (fear, hope); the lighthouse itself (centuries of watching). Credit three perspectives with stories.

Image 2: [A photograph: a girl in a football kit stands alone in a stadium tunnel, looking towards the bright pitch.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a cracked mirror propped against a wall in an empty room; it reflects a doorway, but the doorway is not in the room.]

Choose ONE image. Plan a piece of creative writing: give a title, the form (story, diary, letter or speech), the opening hook, the turning point, the ending and the register you will use.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry or letter; narrator: a first-person child narrator; structure: the last morning – the journey – the first sight of somewhere new; techniques: present tense, lists of things left behind, a hopeful final line. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry or letter; narrator: a first-person child narrator; structure: the last morning – the journey – the first sight of somewhere new; techniques: present tense, lists of things left behind, a hopeful final line. items.stem: Mei writes: "Spell-check catches all errors." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Spell-check misses homophones (their/there), missing words and grammar errors; careful proofreading is needed.
items.markingKey: Spell-check misses homophones (their/there), missing words and grammar errors; careful proofreading is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a girl in a football kit stands alone in a stadium tunnel, looking towards the bright pitch.]

Write a speech or story of about 300 words inspired by this image.
items.answer: Indicative content: a first match after an injury, a trial for a national team, or proving a doubter wrong; structure – doubt in the tunnel – flashback to training – stepping into the light; techniques such as internal monologue, light and dark contrast, a ticking clock; a nervous and expectant mood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: a first match after an injury, a trial for a national team, or proving a doubter wrong; structure – doubt in the tunnel – flashback to training – stepping into the light; techniques such as internal monologue, light and dark contrast, a ticking clock; a nervous and expectant mood. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A painting: a lighthouse on a black rock in a storm; its beam cuts across the waves towards a small boat.]

Using this image as a stimulus, write about 300 words told by a first-person narrator.
items.answer: Indicative content: a keeper guiding a boat home, a rescue told from the boat, or a lighthouse that is about to be switched off forever; structure – the storm builds – the boat is seen – the outcome at dawn; techniques such as personification of the sea, light and dark imagery, a cyclical ending; a dramatic and hopeful mood.
